# paigasus-core — `rs/`

## Cargo, the lockfile and nextest

- **Do not remove the macOS `-C strip=none` from `rs/.cargo/config.toml` until spec D6 holds
  (SMA-767).** rustc 1.95 strips a release Mach-O with `rust-objcopy`, and that leaves the string
  pool only 4-byte aligned when the indirect symbol count is odd. dyld on macOS 27 then rejects a
  binary linked with SDK 27. The error is "mis-aligned LINKEDIT". Do not add maturin `--strip` or
  `strip = true`. Do not add napi `--strip`. Each one runs `rust-objcopy` again. The crate-local
  `rs/crates/bindings/paigasus-py-bindings/.cargo/config.toml` must agree with the shared file.
  `repo:affected-smoke` A5 and A10 red when a task that reads the crate-local file does not key on it.
  A build with cwd in that crate gets `-C strip=none` twice. Measured: same stroff and size. Keep both.
- **SMA-767 R1, host units: the CI darwin legs set `CARGO_PROFILE_RELEASE_BUILD_OVERRIDE_STRIP=none`.**
  With `--target`, a target rustflag does not reach the host proc macros and build scripts. They
  keep the release strip with `rust-objcopy`, and rustc loads a proc macro with dlopen. Measured
  on macOS 27.2 (`--release --target aarch64-apple-darwin`, both bindings): 29 of 40 host units got
  `-C strip=debuginfo`; with the variable, 0 did. Today all 4 proc-macro dylibs and 11 build
  scripts are aligned. Cost on macOS: +1.1 MB in `target/release`. The variable is set in a
  darwin-only step of `wheels.yml` and `prebuild.yml`, NOT as `[profile.release.build-override]`
  in `rs/Cargo.toml`. Measured in `rust:1.95.0-bookworm` (`cargo build --release --workspace`):
  the profile grew the Linux target dir by 385 MB (1.45 GB to 1.84 GB, proc-macro `.so` files
  159 MB to 351 MB), with the same build time (85 s, 86 s). It also changed the bytes of every
  shipped Linux binary (py `.so` 582016 to 582008 bytes), because the proc-macro hashes change.
  A local `--target` release build on macOS still strips host units. Set the variable for it.
- `cargo nextest` exits non-zero on a workspace with **no tests** — use `--no-tests=pass`.
- Tests that assert on a log line use `paigasus_logging::test_support` (`capture_logs` at TRACE,
  `capture_logs_at(level)`). Turn on its `test-support` feature from `[dev-dependencies]` only,
  never from `[dependencies]`, so that the production binary does not contain it. This is the
  first `[features]` table in a workspace crate; follow the same pattern for a new test-only
  helper. Do not write a new `LogBuffer`. The helper supports `cargo nextest` only (SMA-689).
- `paigasus-iam`'s Docker-backed suites get their retry budget and container-concurrency cap from
  `rs/.config/nextest.toml` (`profile.default`), so **Moon, `moon run …:test`, and a bare
  `cargo nextest` all pick it up** — but `cargo test` does NOT, since nextest config is
  nextest-only. Don't add `--retries` to a Moon task or a doc: that recreates the
  documented-vs-executed split SMA-521 closed. A test that fails every attempt still reds; one
  that passes on a retry is reported FLAKY. The JUnit report itself is NOT on `profile.default` —
  nextest resolves a profile's report path relative to the shared workspace `target/`, so `moon
  ci`'s 15+ concurrent nextest runs would clobber a report left on `default`. It lives on a
  dedicated `[profile.iam]` instead, selected only by `paigasus-iam-rs:test`'s `args: ['--profile',
  'iam']` — CI uploads it as the `nextest-junit` artifact, but a bare `cargo nextest run -p
  paigasus-iam` writes no report at all.
- `paigasus-iam`'s **Docker-backed** suites (74 of its 77 integration binaries) skip when the
  daemon is unreachable, and that skip is deliberately quiet — nextest discards a passing test's
  stderr and Moon discards a passing task's output, so no message can surface there. What makes
  it visible is `tests/docker_preflight.rs`, a canary that FAILS when Docker is unreachable: a
  Docker-less run yields exactly one red instead of 73 silent passes (SMA-538). The policy itself
  lives once, in the dev-only crate `paigasus-test-docker` (SMA-726; IAM's
  `tests/support/docker.rs` only re-exports it), and `repo:iam-docker-policy-single-site` fails
  if a suite in IAM or the gateway hand-rolls its own copy. Two env vars, both parsing
  `1`/`true`/`yes` (anything else, including `0`, is off — unlike `CI`, which is
  presence-based):
  `PAIGASUS_REQUIRE_DOCKER=1` turns every suite's skip into a panic, which is what a FILTERED run
  (`--test relay_pg`, `-E 'test(foo)'`) needs, since the canary is not in that filter.
  `PAIGASUS_SKIP_DOCKER=1` restores skipping everywhere including the canary — it is a
  per-invocation escape hatch for a Docker Hub rate limit or a daemon restart, **not** a
  shell-profile setting, and a `moon run` that greened under it leaves a cached PASS that replays
  after Docker returns, so follow it with `moon run … --force`. `CI` outranks both, so no
  workflow-file env var can green a CI run that tested nothing. A container that fails with a
  REACHABLE daemon is a hard failure by default — including `keycloak_e2e`'s 240s startup
  timeout, which used to be a fast local skip — though `PAIGASUS_SKIP_DOCKER=1` still downgrades
  it to a skip, since that hatch is checked before any classification happens. A stray `CI=false` still counts as "CI present" (the
  check is presence-based, not value-based) — clear it with `env -u CI cargo nextest run -p
  paigasus-iam`.
- The gateway also has Docker-backed suites now (SMA-677). It has a `docker_preflight` canary.
  It has two Redis test binaries in the nextest `docker-containers` group. Its Moon task
  `paigasus-gateway-rs:test` runs on the `heavy-integration` mutex.
- This repo now has **four** CA-bundle config knobs and they do NOT share semantics. `authn.extra_ca_bundle_path`
  and `upstream.openai.extra_ca_bundle_path` (SMA-558) **ADD** to the trust store — reqwest builds one
  `RootCertStore` by unioning `add_root_certificate` calls with the webpki roots and the platform store, so
  the workspace pins BOTH `rustls-tls` and `rustls-tls-native-roots` (dropping the former is not a
  simplification: reqwest accepts an EMPTY platform store silently, and webpki is the floor that stops a bad
  mount becoming a per-request failure). `outbox.publisher.root_ca_bundle` and the gateway's
  `iam.tls.ca_cert_path` **REPLACE** it. The `extra_` prefix is the marker — a fifth knob must pick a side
  and say which in its doc. Anything in an added bundle becomes an **unconstrained** anchor (no `cA` check),
  so it must contain roots only; a self-signed LEAF works too (put its own cert in the bundle) since rustls
  applies no `cA` check to a trust anchor.
- **Standing rule: A task is in A10's scope when its cargo subcommand COMPILES or LINKS and its
  cwd resolves inside `rs/`. The test is "does this file influence the output", not "is it
  strictly required".**
  `rs/.cargo/config.toml` is now an input of every task that runs cargo from `rs/`: all thirteen
  crates' `build`/`build-release`/`test`/`lint`, the three FFI wrapper tasks, and three `repo:*`
  gates that shell out to cargo (`repo:parity-corpus-drift`, `repo:observability-drift`,
  `repo:nats-permissions`). Editing it selects 61 tasks against 3 before — the 52 crate tasks, the
  3 FFI tasks, and 6 `repo:*` gates (those three, plus `repo:actionlint`, `repo:input-liveness`
  and `repo:publish-metadata`, which select on everything). **59 of those declarations are now
  asserted**: 58 by `repo:affected-smoke`'s A10 (`ci/affected-graph/cargo_moon_parity.py`,
  SMA-599, findings key `a10`), and `paigasus-kernel-py:test` by **A5**, not A10 — it is an FFI
  wrapper task, so the `FFI_TASK_INPUTS` splat already demands the file. A10 DOES derive it (as
  `wrapper`, so the verb test passes); what excludes it is the CWD rule — its blob is
  `uv sync --reinstall-package …` with no cd, and its source dir is `py/packages/paigasus-kernel`. A task is in A10's scope when its cargo subcommand COMPILES or LINKS
  (`CONFIG_SENSITIVE_VERBS`, deliberately NOT A8's `LOCK_RESOLVING_VERBS`) AND its cwd resolves
  inside `rs/` — crate tasks and the `repo:*` gates that reach cargo through their own
  `ci/**/run.sh` alike. `repo:deny` and `repo:machete` are out of scope BY VERB, not on the cwd
  half: `deny` is in `LOCK_RESOLVING_VERBS` and IS derived, but is absent from
  `CONFIG_SENSITIVE_VERBS`, so `_cwd_inside_rs` is never called for it; `machete` is absent from
  `LOCK_RESOLVING_VERBS` entirely and is never derived at all. (`repo:machete` also runs
  `cargo machete rs`, a bare path ARGUMENT, not `--manifest-path`.) The `--manifest-path` fact
  belongs to `repo:deny`, and it is still load-bearing for A10's design decision D2 — MEASURED on
  cargo 1.95.0, a malformed `rs/.cargo/config.toml` fails cwd=rs/ at rc 101 but leaves
  cwd=root+`--manifest-path` at rc 0, so `--manifest-path` does not move cargo's config walk and
  a bare `rs`-containing argument must never confer a cwd. A10 reads moon's RESOLVED inputs, so
  its four inherited lines in `.moon/tasks/rust.yml` (`build`/`build-release`/`test`/`lint`) each
  cover thirteen crates — deleting one reds thirteen tasks. A10 ships with an EMPTY allowlist;
  every exclusion is structural. It is deliberately
  NOT on `fmt`: `cargo fmt --check` neither compiles nor links, so rustflags cannot change its result.
  `repo:wasm-getrandom-free` is excluded for the same kind of reason — it runs `cargo tree`, which
  resolves the dependency graph and never applies rustflags. This REVERSES SMA-546's deliberate
  exclusion, which reasoned that CI is Linux and the darwin flags are inert there. Both are true;
  the criterion changed to "does this file influence the output" rather than "is it strictly
  required", because `rustflags` affect every darwin build from `rs/`. Note maturin injects the
  `-undefined dynamic_lookup` args ITSELF (SMA-578), so the py wheel does not NEED the file — it
  is keyed on it anyway, under the same one rule, which is why `REQUIRED_FFI_TASKS` needs no
  carve-out.
- **A10 enforces the cargo-config rule; nothing enforces the GENERAL one.** A10
  (`ci/affected-graph/cargo_moon_parity.py`, SMA-599) closes the `rs/.cargo/config.toml` case
  specifically, including for a gate that reaches cargo only through its own `ci/**/run.sh` —
  that whole class was outside A8 too until SMA-599. It does not close the general problem: A10
  shares `derive_cargo_tasks`'s VERB LIST, `LOCK_RESOLVING_VERBS`, with A8's derivation, so a
  subcommand outside that list (`cargo llvm-cov`, `insta`, `udeps`, `bloat`) yields an empty
  derivation and stays invisible to A10 too (spec L11). **SMA-605** widened what counts as an
  INVOCATION without touching that verb list: `cargo_matches` merges the literal arm with a
  cargo-NAMED variable in command position (`"$CARGO_BIN" build`) and the `CARGO=<path> <tool>`
  env prefix, the latter carrying wrapper semantics — no flag can ever clear it, since the flag
  reaches the tool and not the cargo behind it. SMA-605 also made script-following TRANSITIVE
  over `source`/`.` statements (cycle-guarded, repo-confined, floored by
  `REQUIRED_SOURCED_SCRIPTS`), which is what finally reaches
  `ci/release-parity/ecosystems/*.sh`; bare `ci/**/*.sh` MENTIONS stay unfollowed, measured at
  six prose edges (comments and pin arrays) and zero true positives. Arm 1 reports ZERO rows on
  the corpus and is labelled forward cover in the code; arm 2 reports one, at
  `ci/release-parity/ecosystems/release-plz.sh:156`, waived because it runs against a
  `mktemp -d` fixture outside the repo. What is still true: A4 covers each
  crate's `lint`/`fmt`, A5 the three derived FFI tasks, and `repo:input-liveness` proves

# paigasus-core — `rs/`

<!-- Project memory. Claude Code loads this file only when it reads a file in

The root CLAUDE.md holds the repo-wide rules and the two gate-checked blocks. -->

## Cargo, the lockfile and nextest

- **Do not remove the macOS `-C strip=none` from `rs/.cargo/config.toml` until spec D6 holds
  (SMA-767).** rustc 1.95 strips a release Mach-O with `rust-objcopy`, and that leaves the string
  pool only 4-byte aligned when the indirect symbol count is odd. dyld on macOS 27 then rejects a
  binary linked with SDK 27. The error is "mis-aligned LINKEDIT". Do not add maturin `--strip` or
  `strip = true`. Do not add napi `--strip`. Each one runs `rust-objcopy` again. The crate-local
  `rs/crates/bindings/paigasus-py-bindings/.cargo/config.toml` must agree with the shared file.
  `repo:affected-smoke` A5 and A10 red when a task that reads the crate-local file does not key on it.
  A build with cwd in that crate gets `-C strip=none` twice. Measured: same stroff and size. Keep both.
- **SMA-767 R1, host units: the CI darwin legs set `CARGO_PROFILE_RELEASE_BUILD_OVERRIDE_STRIP=none`.**
  With `--target`, a target rustflag does not reach the host proc macros and build scripts. They
  keep the release strip with `rust-objcopy`, and rustc loads a proc macro with dlopen. Measured
  on macOS 27.2 (`--release --target aarch64-apple-darwin`, both bindings): 29 of 40 host units got
  `-C strip=debuginfo`; with the variable, 0 did. Today all 4 proc-macro dylibs and 11 build
  scripts are aligned. Cost on macOS: +1.1 MB in `target/release`. The variable is set in a
  darwin-only step of `wheels.yml` and `prebuild.yml`, NOT as `[profile.release.build-override]`
  in `rs/Cargo.toml`. Measured in `rust:1.95.0-bookworm` (`cargo build --release --workspace`):
  the profile grew the Linux target dir by 385 MB (1.45 GB to 1.84 GB, proc-macro `.so` files
  159 MB to 351 MB), with the same build time (85 s, 86 s). It also changed the bytes of every
  shipped Linux binary (py `.so` 582016 to 582008 bytes), because the proc-macro hashes change.
  A local `--target` release build on macOS still strips host units. Set the variable for it.
- `cargo nextest` exits non-zero on a workspace with **no tests** — use `--no-tests=pass`.
- Tests that assert on a log line use `paigasus_logging::test_support` (`capture_logs` at TRACE,
  `capture_logs_at(level)`). Turn on its `test-support` feature from `[dev-dependencies]` only,
  never from `[dependencies]`, so that the production binary does not contain it. This is the
  first `[features]` table in a workspace crate; follow the same pattern for a new test-only
  helper. Do not write a new `LogBuffer`. The helper supports `cargo nextest` only (SMA-689).
- `paigasus-iam`'s Docker-backed suites get their retry budget and container-concurrency cap from
  `rs/.config/nextest.toml` (`profile.default`), so **Moon, `moon run …:test`, and a bare
  `cargo nextest` all pick it up** — but `cargo test` does NOT, since nextest config is
  nextest-only. Don't add `--retries` to a Moon task or a doc: that recreates the
  documented-vs-executed split SMA-521 closed. A test that fails every attempt still reds; one
  that passes on a retry is reported FLAKY. The JUnit report itself is NOT on `profile.default` —
  nextest resolves a profile's report path relative to the shared workspace `target/`, so `moon
  ci`'s 15+ concurrent nextest runs would clobber a report left on `default`. It lives on a
  dedicated `[profile.iam]` instead, selected only by `paigasus-iam-rs:test`'s `args: ['--profile',
  'iam']` — CI uploads it as the `nextest-junit` artifact, but a bare `cargo nextest run -p
  paigasus-iam` writes no report at all.
- `paigasus-iam`'s **Docker-backed** suites (74 of its 77 integration binaries) skip when the
  daemon is unreachable, and that skip is deliberately quiet — nextest discards a passing test's
  stderr and Moon discards a passing task's output, so no message can surface there. What makes
  it visible is `tests/docker_preflight.rs`, a canary that FAILS when Docker is unreachable: a
  Docker-less run yields exactly one red instead of 73 silent passes (SMA-538). The policy itself
  lives once, in the dev-only crate `paigasus-test-docker` (SMA-726; IAM's
  `tests/support/docker.rs` only re-exports it), and `repo:iam-docker-policy-single-site` fails
  if a suite in IAM or the gateway hand-rolls its own copy. Two env vars, both parsing
  `1`/`true`/`yes` (anything else, including `0`, is off — unlike `CI`, which is
  presence-based):
  `PAIGASUS_REQUIRE_DOCKER=1` turns every suite's skip into a panic, which is what a FILTERED run

     Then run the test. If the five artifacts changed, stage, commit and push them as in
     step 4.
  6. For a `Cargo.lock` conflict, do not edit the lock by hand. Comment `@dependabot recreate`.
     Dependabot then writes a new lock on the current `main`. This deletes the glue commit.
     Wait for the new head commit. Then run `gh pr checkout <N> --force` and do step 4 again.
  The merge-only `update-branch` call:
  `gh api -X PUT repos/<owner>/<repo>/pulls/<N>/update-branch -f expected_head_sha=<sha>`.
  Except in step 6, never use `--rebase`, `@dependabot recreate` or `[dependabot skip]`. Each one
  deletes the glue commit.
  A conflict or a merge can let git replace the five files. That breaks the pnpm hard link. Run
  `rm -rf ts/node_modules && pnpm -C ts install` after (ts/CLAUDE.md rule).
  Finish before the next Monday 06:00 UTC dependabot run (INFERRED). A new run can supersede a
  grouped PR.
- **binaryen's `wasm-opt` is pinned in the crate, not in the root `.prototools` (SMA-435).** The
  pin is `rs/crates/bindings/paigasus-wasm/.prototools`, and the plugin is
  `.proto/plugins/binaryen.toml`. proto reads `.prototools` files upwards from the working
  directory. So the bare `proto install` of `ci.yml` at the repository root does not read the pin.
  CI does not download the 111 MB Linux tarball. `ts/packages/paigasus-kernel/scripts/optimize-wasm.mjs`
  runs every `proto` call from the crate directory, runs `wasm-opt -O`, and appends a
  `paigasus.wasm-opt` marker section. `generate-wasm` (the committed binary) and `prebuild.yml`
  (the published binary) call it.
  - To bump binaryen: change the version in the nested `.prototools`, run
    `moon run paigasus-kernel-ts:generate-wasm`, and commit the five artifacts. Check 5 of
    `tests/committed-wasm.test.ts` fails until you do.
  - Never optimize a binary two times. `wasm-opt -O` is deterministic but not idempotent: a second
    run changes the bytes again. The script refuses an input that has the marker or that has no
    `name` section.
  - Never remove `wasm-opt = false` from the `release` or the `profiling` profile in
    `paigasus-wasm/Cargo.toml`. wasm-pack then downloads a binaryen that no file pins. Checks 6
    and 7 fail.
  - The first `proto install wasm-opt` adds `~/.proto/shims/wasm-opt` to the shim-first `PATH` of the
    developer. Outside this crate directory the shim has no configured version. So another wasm-pack
    project on the same host can find this shim instead of its own binaryen.

## Container images

- Container images (SMA-500) live behind
  `ci/images/run.sh {build,smoke,all,build-oci,load-oci,rehearse,context-check}` and
  `.github/workflows/images.yml`, **not** Moon — a `repo:*` task would have to join `ci.yml`'s
  `T=(…)` array (a `--release` build on every affected PR) or become a `T_EXEMPT` entry.
  The console images (SMA-513) use the same script: `build-console [iam|gateway]` and
  `all-consoles`. The workflow is **not a required check**. So a broken image build makes
  `main` red, not the PR.
- The `pull_request` filter of `images.yml` lists the image build inputs. For `rs/` these are
  `rs/Dockerfile`, `rs/docker/**` (the chisel dpkg status generator, its self-test and its
  fixtures, SMA-665), `rs/Cargo.{lock,toml}`, `rs/rust-toolchain.toml` and `rs/.dockerignore`. For
  `ts/` these are `ts/Dockerfile`, `ts/.dockerignore`, `ts/pnpm-lock.yaml`,
  `ts/pnpm-workspace.yaml`, `ts/package.json`, `ts/.npmrc`, `ts/apps/*/lib/config.ts`,
  `ts/apps/*/next.config.ts`, `ts/apps/*/package.json`,
  and `ts/packages/paigasus-kernel/package.json`. It also lists four smoke-runtime files
  (SMA-675, the second clause of RUNBOOK-containers.md section 1):
  `ts/packages/paigasus-auth/src/core/session.ts`, `ts/apps/*/app/*console*/layout.tsx`,
  `ts/apps/iam-console/app/*console*/orgs/page.tsx` and
  `ts/apps/gateway-console/app/*console*/overview/page.tsx`. It also lists `ci/images/**`, the
  workflow, `.prototools`, `.proto/plugins/crane.toml` and `.proto/plugins/syft.toml`. A PR that changes one of these
  runs the workflow automatically. The rule for a `ts/` entry is in RUNBOOK-containers.md section 1.

  it too, because a bad edit there already reds the ordinary `moon ci` build — this is why the
  five committed wasm artifacts, `paigasus-wasm/package.json`,
  `paigasus-node-bindings/package.json` and the napi crate's `index.js`/`index.d.ts` are absent.
  The two napi glue files are `paigasus-kernel-ts:test` inputs since SMA-667, and
  `tests/committed-napi-glue.test.ts` holds them to the generator.
  `@paigasus/next-config` is off the filter too (SMA-671): it is a Moon input, the unit tests and
  `standalone-runtime.test.ts` pin both base paths, and `chart.yml` is the second control.

  listed input can still break an image build. Start the workflow manually for such a PR with
  `workflow_dispatch`. (`gh workflow run images.yml --ref <branch>` returns 404 until `images.yml`
  is on `main`.)

  host build of both consoles on each leg and sets `CONSOLE_PARITY_REQUIRED: '1'` on its two
  console smoke steps; unset means "not required", so `release.yml` needs no host build. It gates
  amd64 on a filtered PR and both legs on `main`. A PR that changes only `ts/apps/*/moon.yml` does
  not run it, so a `moon.yml`-side staging drift shows first on `main`. Row W1 of
  `ci/images/console-selftest.sh` pins the two `env` lines and the step order.

  measured: `libgcc-s1_libs` is REQUIRED (Rust panic unwinding links `libgcc_s.so.1`) and its
  absence fails at container START, not build; `ca-certificates_data` is the right variant
  (`-with-certs` adds ~120 PEMs nothing reads); there is **no `/etc/passwd`**, so `USER` must be
  numeric; and `chisel cut --root DIR` does not create `DIR`. `/etc/nsswitch.conf` is also absent
  and that is FINE — glibc falls back to a compiled-in `files dns` default and the NSS modules
  ship in `libc6_libs`. The smoke suite pins this by reaching Postgres at a CONTAINER
  HOSTNAME rather than an IP literal; public-name resolution was verified once by hand during
  design and is NOT covered continuously.

  behind a pinned-looking `FROM`. `rs/Dockerfile` sets `RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN` and

{"id":"SMA-757","uuid":"72428d42-2e2a-40ca-9ec2-9abae86df97a","title":"Gateway: tighten the oracle's argument-prefix check before argument-based policies","description":"The differential oracle from <issue id="5873cf2f-f707-4ec8-a57d-c418a90fd209" label="SMA-749" href="https://linear.app/smaschek/issue/SMA-749/gateway-provider-neutral-tool-call-model-and-toolcallassembler-for" /> accepts a client result whose arguments are a **prefix** of the decided arguments, when the client raised partway through a call. That is sound only while deciders look at the tool name alone, which is true today (`AllowAll`).

With <issue id="466c1119-3b29-488b-b0df-1aa3851823c8" label="SMA-752" href="https://linear.app/smaschek/issue/SMA-752/gateway-and-kernel-invoketool-decisions-with-log-only-and-enforce" />, policies can read arguments. Then a prefix of allowed arguments may itself be a call that policy would deny, and the oracle would not notice.

## Done when

* The oracle accepts a partial result only when the policy verdict for the partial arguments is the same as for the full ones, or it rejects any partial client result outright.
* A property test with an argument-reading decider fails on the current tolerance and passes after the change.
* This lands before, or as part of, <issue id="466c1119-3b29-488b-b0df-1aa3851823c8" label="SMA-752" href="https://linear.app/smaschek/issue/SMA-752/gateway-and-kernel-invoketool-decisions-with-log-only-and-enforce" />.

# paigasus-core — `rs/`

## Cargo, the lockfile and nextest

- **Do not remove the macOS `-C strip=none` from `rs/.cargo/config.toml` until spec D6 holds

  binary linked with SDK 27. The error is "mis-aligned LINKEDIT". Do not add maturin `--strip` or
  `strip = true`. Do not add napi `--strip`. Each one runs `rust-objcopy` again. The crate-local
  `rs/crates/bindings/paigasus-py-bindings/.cargo/config.toml` must agree with the shared file.
  `repo:affected-smoke` A5 and A10 red when a task that reads the crate-local file does not key on it.
  A build with cwd in that crate gets `-C strip=none` twice. Measured: same stroff and size. Keep both.
- **SMA-767 R1, host units: the CI darwin legs set `CARGO_PROFILE_RELEASE_BUILD_OVERRIDE_STRIP=none`.**
  With `--target`, a target rustflag does not reach the host proc macros and build scripts. They
  keep the release strip with `rust-objcopy`, and rustc loads a proc macro with dlopen. Measured
  on macOS 27.2 (`--release --target aarch64-apple-darwin`, both bindings): 29 of 40 host units got
  `-C strip=debuginfo`; with the variable, 0 did. Today all 4 proc-macro dylibs and 11 build
  scripts are aligned. Cost on macOS: +1.1 MB in `target/release`. The variable is set in a
  darwin-only step of `wheels.yml` and `prebuild.yml`, NOT as `[profile.release.build-override]`
  in `rs/Cargo.toml`. Measured in `rust:1.95.0-bookworm` (`cargo build --release --workspace`):
  the profile grew the Linux target dir by 385 MB (1.45 GB to 1.84 GB, proc-macro `.so` files
  159 MB to 351 MB), with the same build time (85 s, 86 s). It also changed the bytes of every
  shipped Linux binary (py `.so` 582016 to 582008 bytes), because the proc-macro hashes change.
  A local `--target` release build on macOS still strips host units. Set the variable for it.
- `cargo nextest` exits non-zero on a workspace with **no tests** — use `--no-tests=pass`.
- Tests that assert on a log line use `paigasus_logging::test_support` (`capture_logs` at TRACE,
  `capture_logs_at(level)`). Turn on its `test-support` feature from `[dev-dependencies]` only,
  never from `[dependencies]`, so that the production binary does not contain it. This is the
  first `[features]` table in a workspace crate; follow the same pattern for a new test-only
  helper. Do not write a new `LogBuffer`. The helper supports `cargo nextest` only (SMA-689).
- `paigasus-iam`'s Docker-backed suites get their retry budget and container-concurrency cap from
  `rs/.config/nextest.toml` (`profile.default`), so **Moon, `moon run …:test`, and a bare
  `cargo nextest` all pick it up** — but `cargo test` does NOT, since nextest config is
  nextest-only. Don't add `--retries` to a Moon task or a doc: that recreates the
  documented-vs-executed split SMA-521 closed. A test that fails every attempt still reds; one
  that passes on a retry is reported FLAKY. The JUnit report itself is NOT on `profile.default` —
  nextest resolves a profile's report path relative to the shared workspace `target/`, so `moon
  ci`'s 15+ concurrent nextest runs would clobber a report left on `default`. It lives on a
  dedicated `[profile.iam]` instead, selected only by `paigasus-iam-rs:test`'s `args: ['--profile',
  'iam']` — CI uploads it as the `nextest-junit` artifact, but a bare `cargo nextest run -p
  paigasus-iam` writes no report at all.
- `paigasus-iam`'s **Docker-backed** suites (74 of its 77 integration binaries) skip when the
  daemon is unreachable, and that skip is deliberately quiet — nextest discards a passing test's
  stderr and Moon discards a passing task's output, so no message can surface there. What makes
  it visible is `tests/docker_preflight.rs`, a canary that FAILS when Docker is unreachable: a
  Docker-less run yields exactly one red instead of 73 silent passes (SMA-538). The policy itself

  `tests/support/docker.rs` only re-exports it), and `repo:iam-docker-policy-single-site` fails

content.content:
`extra_ca_bundle_path` exist for self-hosted vLLM / LiteLLM (SMA-558). Such upstreams
  interleave indices, emit odd framing, or can be made to emit arbitrary bytes. Nothing about
  the upstream's framing or JSON is trusted.
- T3. **The caller is not an adversary of its own agent** in this spec. Request-side
  differentials (for example duplicate `tools` keys) are SMA-752's concern.

**Invariant (I1).** For every supported client parser P (§ 8.2), every tool call that P
accumulates from the bytes the gateway emits was decided `Allow`, with the same choice, kind,
name and arguments that the decider saw. Anything the gateway cannot classify with certainty
is not forwarded (or triggers `on_failure`).

**Non-goals.** Tool calls encoded inside text content (ReAct / XML conventions, or a vLLM tool
parser that fails and falls back to `content`); tools executed by the provider (Anthropic
`server_tool_use`, `mcp_tool_use`); the OpenAI Responses API; request rewriting.

## 3. Decisions

| Id | Question | Decision |
|----|----------|----------|
| D1 | Where the code lives | New crate `paigasus-gateway-core` (`publish = false`): types, SSE framing, JSON classification, assembly, rewrite, as a sans-IO state machine. `paigasus-gateway` drives it with tokio. No kernel change in this spec. |
| D2 | SSE input framing | WHATWG line splitting (CR, LF, CRLF), with a CR held until the next byte. Strip one leading UTF-8 BOM. Multi-line `data:` joined with `\n`. |
  `"Tool_Calls"` a tool call to them. `__proto__` can change the accumulated object in
  JavaScript. Rejecting all of these costs nothing on a conforming upstream.
- **D6, positive allowlist.** "Has a `tool_calls` key" is wrong both ways. It misses
  `tool_calls` as an object or string and `message.tool_calls` inside a chunk. It also holds
  all text on upstreams that send `"tool_calls": []` on every delta (some vLLM versions).
- **D9, canonical assembly.** The SDKs disagree. openai-python concatenates every string field
  except `index` and `type`, so a second `name` fragment becomes `safe_` + `rm`. openai-node
  replaces it. anthropic-python appends a block on start but applies deltas by index. The
  decider must see what every client will run, and that is only knowable for the canonical
  form.
- **D10/D11, truncation.** The relay turns a transport error into a data record and a clean
  end. An assembler placed after that conversion would see EOF and release a call cut off
  mid-arguments. D17 moves the state machine in front of the conversion.
- **D12, one FIFO.** Per-choice holds with a shared tail leak: releasing hold A would ship
  frames of hold B sitting in A's tail. A frame can also carry several choices. Keeping the
  stream order and releasing only fully decided frames is the simplest rule that never leaks.

- `text`, `thinking`, `redacted_thinking`: tool-free content.
- `server_tool_use`, `*_tool_result`, `mcp_tool_use`: tool-free, reported `unenforceable`.
- `tool_use`: tool-bearing.
- any other block type: tool-bearing, kind `Other` (fail closed).

### 4.3 Canonical assembly (any deviation → stream-level `on_failure`, code `Malformed`)

OpenAI, per choice:

- tool-call `index` values first appear in order 0, 1, 2, …; interleaving after that is fine;
- `id`, `type` and `function.name` (or `custom.name`) each appear in exactly one fragment;
- `type` never changes, and `function` and `custom` never appear in the same entry;
- `function.arguments` and `custom.input` are strings or `null` in every fragment (`null` adds
  nothing, as in every SDK);
- at the call's completion, `function.arguments` (Function and legacy calls) is `""` or one
  complete JSON value (§ 11, `incomplete_arguments`); `custom.input` is free text;
- a legacy `function_call` and `tool_calls` never appear in the same choice;
- no fragment arrives for a call after its choice's `finish_reason`.

### 8.1 Differential oracle (the security proof)

`tests/oracle/` holds Rust models of these client accumulators:

- openai-python `accumulate_delta` / `ChatCompletionStreamState`;
- openai-node `ChatCompletionStream`;

# Brainstorming

You are very good at building. You build what you believe your human
partner wants, and that belief is usually thinner than it feels. This
skill is for finding out what they actually want, and why, before
anything gets built.

People often haven't finished working out what they want. Good questions
help them think it through. When you understand the why, you make the
hundred decisions they never mention the way they would have made them.

## First: What Do You Actually Know?

Before you reply, ask yourself: what do I know about what they want, and
why?

- **Everything that matters is in the request** ("make the icon cornflower
  blue"). This is a quick, clear task. Do it, and say what you did.
- **Something non-trivial is missing.** Start the conversation.

Before you start implementing, you must, in order:

1. Lay out the approaches in a message of their own, and have your
   human partner pick one (see Lay out the approaches).
2. Write the design doc, short or full (see Size the Work).
3. Get their approval of that doc.
4. Invoke the superpowers:writing-plans skill.

If nothing is open when you write your first message and there's one
sensible way, steps 1 to 3 happen in that message (see Your First
Message).

Two things aren't implementing: a spike they said yes to (see Spike to
feel things out), and doing what they asked once they've opted out of
the questions.

## Look Before You Ask

In an existing project, or when they've given you context (a spec, a plan,
a handoff, files they pointed at, earlier conversation), dig in before your
first message. Read what they referred to and the code or material it
connects to, and keep reading until you can explain how the relevant
parts work today and what this change would touch. Never ask what the
project or their context already answers, or reopen what they've
already decided.

## Your First Message

Move the work forward, with one of these:

- **They've already said what they want** (a spec, a plan, a detailed
  request): aim for about 200 words for the whole message. Echo their
  request back in your own words, so they can see whether you've got its
  shape: what they want, who it's for, and why, as far as they've said.
  Add what you found that bears on it: how the relevant parts work today
  and what the change would touch. If you found something they may not
  have considered that would change what they're asking for or how it
  has to be built, like a constraint, a conflict, or a cheaper path, say
  so plainly. How to build it comes later, once you understand what they
  want (see Lay out the approaches). End with one line inviting
  corrections. Then, if they haven't told you why they want it, even if
  you can guess, ask about that: one open question in their own terms,
  with nothing to pick from. If they have told you, and their request
  and the project leave open something whose answer would change what
  gets built, ask about the one that would change it most; when its
  choices can be named, sketch each concretely, with what it trades off
  and which you'd pick. If nothing like that is open, there's one
  sensible way: end with the short design itself (the approach, a line on
  why the others don't fit, and the design in a few lines) and ask them
  to approve it. Their approval covers the approach and the design: write
  the short design doc as approved and go on to the plan.
  Specs are often incomplete, so confirm before you build on one.
- **They haven't:** one open question, in their own terms, about the
  biggest thing their request leaves unsettled. Say why you're asking:
  what the answer would change about what you build. For "a website for
  my bakery": "If it's mostly for people deciding whether to stop by,
  I'd lead with hours and what's in the case today; taking orders is a
  different site. What do you want someone to do when they land on it?"

How the message ends depends on whether their message asked for
brainstorming:

- **They asked for it** (by name, by invoking it, or by asking for a
  design discussion): end there. They want this conversation.
- **They didn't:** they may not want a conversation at all. End with a
  light, one-line offer to just get going instead, like
  "Or if you'd rather I just dive in, say so." If they take you up on
  it, this skill is done: state any significant how-it-gets-made choice
  (platform, language, medium) in one plain line, then do what they
  asked through the normal workflow.

That's the whole message.

## The Conversation

Ask a question only when the answer would change what gets built and
neither the request nor the project answers it. Otherwise, state your
call and your reason as a proposal they can correct, and move the work
forward. Process steps are always your calls: writing things up, where
files go, looking further, how to show something. Do them and say so.
Ask one at a time. Use plain language, pitched just a little above where
your human partner is. Match their vocabulary; never use process jargon.
You never need to quote this skill to your human partner.

Be clear and concise. Lead with what matters. Avoid jargon. When you
report what you found, give them the most important findings and offer
the rest.

**Get them describing.** Until you know why they want it, ask open
questions, with no example answers attached. Their own words carry
intent that your options can't. Once you know why, when a decision has
choices you can name, sketch each concretely, with what it trades off
and which you'd pick. When they say "just guess" or "what do you think?",
propose something concrete.

**How it gets made.** Every project rests on choices about medium, tools,
materials, and resources: the platform, programming language, and
libraries for an app; the medium for a piece of art. Read from how they
talk which of those choices they want to make. Someone who raises the how
or asks about trade-offs wants the options with your pick. Someone who
talks about outcomes is handing you the how: make those calls and state
each in a line. When there's existing work, build on what it already
uses. Any choice you make goes in the design as your call, never as
something they agreed to.

**Ground to cover.** This is territory, not a script. Never read these
out as questions:

- what kind of thing this is, and what makes it special
- why now, and what success looks like to them
- goals, non-goals, and anti-goals (what would make this a failure even
  if it technically works)
- prior art: what they've seen elsewhere, loved or hated
- current state: what exists now, what they've tried
- the details they care about

**Make every question specific** to their project and what they've told
you. Ask Socratically, the way a sharp colleague would: build each
question on their last answer or on something you found, so it helps
them think through a consequence or a case they may have missed
("Voting closes before the meeting, and two members joined this month.
Does someone who joins mid-round get a vote?"). When the reason isn't
already plain, say what you're hoping to learn or what the answer would
change. A proposal they can correct, plus your reason for it, often
beats a question.

**Do recon.** Once you have a bit of grounding and looking further
would help, go look: deeper into their codebase or project, their own
files and data, or the web. Say what you looked for and what you found.

**Lay out the approaches.** Once you understand what they want, and
before you write anything up, put the ways of building it in a message
of its own. Come up with several real alternatives and drop the weak
ones, including any that work against why they want it and any the
existing work rules out. Sketch the two or three that remain concretely
enough to picture, grounded in what the project actually does, with what
each trades off. Recommend one and say why, then ask which way they want
to go; if they've handed you the how, say you'll go with your pick
instead. When there's genuinely one sensible way, say so in that
message and explain why the others don't fit; the design comes in the
next one. This is for how it gets built; for what they want, get them
describing first.

**Show, don't tell.** Whenever seeing would help more than reading,
sketch it in text: a few lines of what they'd see. Offer the visual
companion (below) when the look itself is theirs to decide:

- something they'll look at: a screen, a page, a printout, a sign
- a layout or arrangement: of a screen, a room, a schedule
- a flow or a sequence of steps
- options that would look different from each other
- a structure that's easier to see than read: a diagram, a timeline, a map

Once they've accepted, use it for mockups to react to, side-by-side
options, and throwaway prototypes they can click.

**Spike to feel things out.** Agentic work is waterfall, but very, very
fast. A quick throwaway build is often the cheapest way to learn what
they want or whether something works. Offer one when it would help.
When they just want to spike, get out of the way. Spikes get no tests
or minimal ones, aren't bulletproof, and skip the plan, implementation,
and review process. Bring what the spike taught you back into the
conversation.

## Play It Back

Play back as you go. As soon as you understand one part well enough to
describe it (what it's for and who it serves, say, or how one piece
behaves), describe that part back in about 200-300 words, then return to
questions about the next part. Playback and questions alternate through
the whole conversation; the last chunk covers whatever is left.

Only what they said goes in as theirs. Anything you filled in goes in
as your proposal, with your reason. End each chunk by asking what's wrong
or missing.

Before you send a chunk, check it: does it describe something they'll
look at, like a page, a screen, a schedule, or a printout? If so, put a
text sketch next to the description. If the look itself is theirs to
decide and they haven't seen the visual companion offer yet, send the
offer instead (its own message, below) and hold the chunk for the next
message. Once they've accepted, put a mockup next to the description.

## Size the Work

Once you understand what they want and they've picked an approach, say
how big the work is in plain words. They can override it.

| Size | The design doc |
|------|----------------|
| A small change | a short one: what you already covered together, written down |
| A project | the full written design (below) |

Short or full, the design doc has an **Approaches** part: the two or
three ways you considered building it, what each trades off, which one
they picked, and why. They pick in the conversation, before you write
the doc.

If it grows mid-task, stop, say so, and step up a size.

If this is really several independent projects, say so, agree on an
order, and brainstorm them one at a time.

## The Written Design

Write a plain document a talented builder in the domain could plan
from without going back to your human partner. Cover:

- intent and the why
- goals, non-goals, anti-goals
- constraints
- approaches (above)
- the parts of the how they decided, as they decided them
- what's left to the builder

For a small change, the short design covers the same points in a line
or two each and goes straight to your human partner, without the
builder check.

**Where it goes:** in a software repo,
`docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`, committed.
Otherwise, pick a sensible place and say where. Your human partner's
preferences override both.

**Builder check** (for a project): dispatch a fresh subagent with
`builder-check-prompt.md` in this directory. When you tell your human
partner you're writing it up, say a reviewer will read it first and you
may come back once with a few questions. Don't hand over the document
until the check is back. Sort what the builder asks into three piles:

- **Answered already** by the conversation or the project: put the answer
  in the document.
- **Minor:** a sensible builder could settle it without changing what gets
  built. Settle it yourself and mark it in the document as your call.
- **Theirs:** only your human partner can answer it, and the answer changes
  what gets built.

Bring the "theirs" pile in one message, most important first. Update the
document with their answers, then hand it over with a short list of the
calls you made so they can check those while reading. That's the only
round of questions the check produces. Without a subagent tool, read the
document as that builder yourself.

<HARD-GATE>
Nothing gets built until your human partner approves the design doc:
the short one for a small change, the full one for a project.
Building includes writing product code, scaffolding, installing
dependencies, creating projects, and invoking an implementation skill.
Reading and exploring are fine.

Two exceptions. If they opted out of the questions, the skill is done
and the gate goes with it. A spike they said yes to may be built; it
stays labeled throwaway, and keeping what it produced is a new request
that comes back through this gate.

After the design doc is approved, the next step is the plan: invoke
superpowers:writing-plans and no other skill.
</HARD-GATE>

## Red Flags

| Thought | Reality |
|---------|---------|
| "I'll offer a menu of what they might want" | Options steer. Ask them to describe it first. |
| "I'll fill in sensible defaults" | Good. Say them out loud. A default they never heard is one they couldn't reject. |
| "I've answered their questions, so I'll write the doc" | Lay out the approaches first, in a message of their own (or, when nothing was open from the start, in your first message's short design). |
| "I should explain the process first" | Ask your question. The process shows itself. |
| "They said 'sounds good' to the idea" | Approval covers what you showed them. A design doc you haven't written isn't approved. |
| "The spike works, I'll keep building on it" | Keeping it is a new request. Back through the gate. |

## Visual Companion

A browser tab for showing mockups, diagrams, and prototypes. It's a
tool, not a mode: accepting it doesn't send every question to the
browser.

**Offer it just-in-time.** Offer it the first time one of the moments
above comes up, never upfront. The offer is its own message with nothing
else in it:

> "This might be easier if I show you. Want me to open a browser tab with some mockups?"

If they decline, stay in text and don't offer again unless they raise it.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/smaschek/.claude/plugins/cache/claude-plugins-official/superpowers/7.0.2/skills/brainstorming

# Brainstorming

You are very good at building. You build what you believe your human
partner wants, and that belief is usually thinner than it feels. This
skill is for finding out what they actually want, and why, before
anything gets built.

People often haven't finished working out what they want. Good questions
help them think it through. When you understand the why, you make the
hundred decisions they never mention the way they would have made them.

## First: What Do You Actually Know?

Before you reply, ask yourself: what do I know about what they want, and
why?

- **Everything that matters is in the request** ("make the icon cornflower
  blue"). This is a quick, clear task. Do it, and say what you did.
- **Something non-trivial is missing.** Start the conversation.

Before you start implementing, you must, in order:

1. Lay out the approaches in a message of their own, and have your
   human partner pick one (see Lay out the approaches).
2. Write the design doc, short or full (see Size the Work).
3. Get their approval of that doc.
4. Invoke the superpowers:writing-plans skill.

If nothing is open when you write your first message and there's one
sensible way, steps 1 to 3 happen in that message (see Your First
Message).

Two things aren't implementing: a spike they said yes to (see Spike to
feel things out), and doing what they asked once they've opted out of
the questions.

## Look Before You Ask

In an existing project, or when they've given you context (a spec, a plan,
a handoff, files they pointed at, earlier conversation), dig in before your
first message. Read what they referred to and the code or material it
connects to, and keep reading until you can explain how the relevant
parts work today and what this change would touch. Never ask what the
project or their context already answers, or reopen what they've
already decided.

## Your First Message

Move the work forward, with one of these:

- **They've already said what they want** (a spec, a plan, a detailed
  request): aim for about 200 words for the whole message. Echo their
  request back in your own words, so they can see whether you've got its
  shape: what they want, who it's for, and why, as far as they've said.
  Add what you found that bears on it: how the relevant parts work today
  and what the change would touch. If you found something they may not
  have considered that would change what they're asking for or how it
  has to be built, like a constraint, a conflict, or a cheaper path, say
  so plainly. How to build it comes later, once you understand what they
  want (see Lay out the approaches). End with one line inviting
  corrections. Then, if they haven't told you why they want it, even if
  you can guess, ask about that: one open question in their own terms,
  with nothing to pick from. If they have told you, and their request
  and the project leave open something whose answer would change what
  gets built, ask about the one that would change it most; when its
  choices can be named, sketch each concretely, with what it trades off
  and which you'd pick. If nothing like that is open, there's one
  sensible way: end with the short design itself (the approach, a line on
  why the others don't fit, and the design in a few lines) and ask them
  to approve it. Their approval covers the approach and the design: write
  the short design doc as approved and go on to the plan.
  Specs are often incomplete, so confirm before you build on one.
- **They haven't:** one open question, in their own terms, about the
  biggest thing their request leaves unsettled. Say why you're asking:
  what the answer would change about what you build. For "a website for
  my bakery": "If it's mostly for people deciding whether to stop by,
  I'd lead with hours and what's in the case today; taking orders is a
  different site. What do you want someone to do when they land on it?"

How the message ends depends on whether their message asked for
brainstorming:

- **They asked for it** (by name, by invoking it, or by asking for a
  design discussion): end there. They want this conversation.
- **They didn't:** they may not want a conversation at all. End with a
  light, one-line offer to just get going instead, like
  "Or if you'd rather I just dive in, say so." If they take you up on
  it, this skill is done: state any significant how-it-gets-made choice
  (platform, language, medium) in one plain line, then do what they
  asked through the normal workflow.

That's the whole message.

## The Conversation

Ask a question only when the answer would change what gets built and
neither the request nor the project answers it. Otherwise, state your
call and your reason as a proposal they can correct, and move the work
forward. Process steps are always your calls: writing things up, where
files go, looking further, how to show something. Do them and say so.
Ask one at a time. Use plain language, pitched just a little above where
your human partner is. Match their vocabulary; never use process jargon.
You never need to quote this skill to your human partner.

Be clear and concise. Lead with what matters. Avoid jargon. When you
report what you found, give them the most important findings and offer
the rest.

**Get them describing.** Until you know why they want it, ask open
questions, with no example answers attached. Their own words carry
intent that your options can't. Once you know why, when a decision has
choices you can name, sketch each concretely, with what it trades off
and which you'd pick. When they say "just guess" or "what do you think?",
propose something concrete.

**How it gets made.** Every project rests on choices about medium, tools,
materials, and resources: the platform, programming language, and
libraries for an app; the medium for a piece of art. Read from how they
talk which of those choices they want to make. Someone who raises the how
or asks about trade-offs wants the options with your pick. Someone who
talks about outcomes is handing you the how: make those calls and state
each in a line. When there's existing work, build on what it already
uses. Any choice you make goes in the design as your call, never as
something they agreed to.

**Ground to cover.** This is territory, not a script. Never read these
out as questions:

- what kind of thing this is, and what makes it special
- why now, and what success looks like to them
- goals, non-goals, and anti-goals (what would make this a failure even
  if it technically works)
- prior art: what they've seen elsewhere, loved or hated
- current state: what exists now, what they've tried
- the details they care about

**Make every question specific** to their project and what they've told
you. Ask Socratically, the way a sharp colleague would: build each
question on their last answer or on something you found, so it helps
them think through a consequence or a case they may have missed
("Voting closes before the meeting, and two members joined this month.
Does someone who joins mid-round get a vote?"). When the reason isn't
already plain, say what you're hoping to learn or what the answer would
change. A proposal they can correct, plus your reason for it, often
beats a question.

**Do recon.** Once you have a bit of grounding and looking further
would help, go look: deeper into their codebase or project, their own
files and data, or the web. Say what you looked for and what you found.

**Lay out the approaches.** Once you understand what they want, and
before you write anything up, put the ways of building it in a message
of its own. Come up with several real alternatives and drop the weak
ones, including any that work against why they want it and any the
existing work rules out. Sketch the two or three that remain concretely
enough to picture, grounded in what the project actually does, with what
each trades off. Recommend one and say why, then ask which way they want
to go; if they've handed you the how, say you'll go with your pick
instead. When there's genuinely one sensible way, say so in that
message and explain why the others don't fit; the design comes in the
next one. This is for how it gets built; for what they want, get them
describing first.

**Show, don't tell.** Whenever seeing would help more than reading,
sketch it in text: a few lines of what they'd see. Offer the visual
companion (below) when the look itself is theirs to decide:

- something they'll look at: a screen, a page, a printout, a sign
- a layout or arrangement: of a screen, a room, a schedule
- a flow or a sequence of steps
- options that would look different from each other
- a structure that's easier to see than read: a diagram, a timeline, a map

Once they've accepted, use it for mockups to react to, side-by-side
options, and throwaway prototypes they can click.

**Spike to feel things out.** Agentic work is waterfall, but very, very
fast. A quick throwaway build is often the cheapest way to learn what
they want or whether something works. Offer one when it would help.
When they just want to spike, get out of the way. Spikes get no tests
or minimal ones, aren't bulletproof, and skip the plan, implementation,
and review process. Bring what the spike taught you back into the
conversation.

## Play It Back

Play back as you go. As soon as you understand one part well enough to
describe it (what it's for and who it serves, say, or how one piece
behaves), describe that part back in about 200-300 words, then return to
questions about the next part. Playback and questions alternate through
the whole conversation; the last chunk covers whatever is left.

Only what they said goes in as theirs. Anything you filled in goes in
as your proposal, with your reason. End each chunk by asking what's wrong
or missing.

Before you send a chunk, check it: does it describe something they'll
look at, like a page, a screen, a schedule, or a printout? If so, put a
text sketch next to the description. If the look itself is theirs to
decide and they haven't seen the visual companion offer yet, send the
offer instead (its own message, below) and hold the chunk for the next
message. Once they've accepted, put a mockup next to the description.

## Size the Work

Once you understand what they want and they've picked an approach, say
how big the work is in plain words. They can override it.

| Size | The design doc |
|------|----------------|
| A small change | a short one: what you already covered together, written down |
| A project | the full written design (below) |

Short or full, the design doc has an **Approaches** part: the two or
three ways you considered building it, what each trades off, which one
they picked, and why. They pick in the conversation, before you write
the doc.

If it grows mid-task, stop, say so, and step up a size.

If this is really several independent projects, say so, agree on an
order, and brainstorm them one at a time.

## The Written Design

Write a plain document a talented builder in the domain could plan
from without going back to your human partner. Cover:

- intent and the why
- goals, non-goals, anti-goals
- constraints
- approaches (above)
- the parts of the how they decided, as they decided them
- what's left to the builder

For a small change, the short design covers the same points in a line
or two each and goes straight to your human partner, without the
builder check.

**Where it goes:** in a software repo,
`docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`, committed.
Otherwise, pick a sensible place and say where. Your human partner's
preferences override both.

**Builder check** (for a project): dispatch a fresh subagent with
`builder-check-prompt.md` in this directory. When you tell your human
partner you're writing it up, say a reviewer will read it first and you
may come back once with a few questions. Don't hand over the document
until the check is back. Sort what the builder asks into three piles:

- **Answered already** by the conversation or the project: put the answer
  in the document.
- **Minor:** a sensible builder could settle it without changing what gets
  built. Settle it yourself and mark it in the document as your call.
- **Theirs:** only your human partner can answer it, and the answer changes
  what gets built.

Bring the "theirs" pile in one message, most important first. Update the
document with their answers, then hand it over with a short list of the
calls you made so they can check those while reading. That's the only
round of questions the check produces. Without a subagent tool, read the
document as that builder yourself.

<HARD-GATE>
Nothing gets built until your human partner approves the design doc:
the short one for a small change, the full one for a project.
Building includes writing product code, scaffolding, installing
dependencies, creating projects, and invoking an implementation skill.
Reading and exploring are fine.

Two exceptions. If they opted out of the questions, the skill is done
and the gate goes with it. A spike they said yes to may be built; it
stays labeled throwaway, and keeping what it produced is a new request
that comes back through this gate.

After the design doc is approved, the next step is the plan: invoke
superpowers:writing-plans and no other skill.
</HARD-GATE>

## Red Flags

| Thought | Reality |
|---------|---------|
| "I'll offer a menu of what they might want" | Options steer. Ask them to describe it first. |
| "I'll fill in sensible defaults" | Good. Say them out loud. A default they never heard is one they couldn't reject. |
| "I've answered their questions, so I'll write the doc" | Lay out the approaches first, in a message of their own (or, when nothing was open from the start, in your first message's short design). |
| "I should explain the process first" | Ask your question. The process shows itself. |
| "They said 'sounds good' to the idea" | Approval covers what you showed them. A design doc you haven't written isn't approved. |
| "The spike works, I'll keep building on it" | Keeping it is a new request. Back through the gate. |

## Visual Companion

A browser tab for showing mockups, diagrams, and prototypes. It's a
tool, not a mode: accepting it doesn't send every question to the
browser.

**Offer it just-in-time.** Offer it the first time one of the moments
above comes up, never upfront. The offer is its own message with nothing
else in it:

> "This might be easier if I show you. Want me to open a browser tab with some mockups?"

If they decline, stay in text and don't offer again unless they raise it.

**Per question, ask: would they understand this better by seeing it?**
Mockups, layouts, diagrams, and side-by-side designs go in the browser.
Requirements, scope, tradeoffs, and conceptual choices stay in text. A
question about a UI topic isn't automatically a visual question.

If they accept, read `visual-companion.md` in this directory before
starting the server.

# SMA-757: verdict-preserving argument prefixes in the oracle, and the interceptor gap they expose

Linear: SMA-757 (parent SMA-747). Related: SMA-749 (the oracle and the interceptor), SMA-752
(argument-reading policies). This change must land before SMA-752 or as part of it.

## 1. Intent

The differential oracle of SMA-749 (`rs/crates/libs/paigasus-gateway-core/tests/support/oracle.rs`)
checks invariant I1: every call that a client model derives from the gateway's output was decided
`Allow`, with the same choice, kind, name and arguments. When a client model raises partway
through a stream, and the raise is excused (`core_failed`, or the client also raises on the
upstream bytes), the oracle accepts a call whose arguments are only a **prefix** of the decided
arguments (`json_prefix` for parsed values, `starts_with` for raw strings).

That tolerance is sound only while deciders read the tool name alone. SMA-752 adds policies that
read arguments. A prefix of allowed arguments can then be a call that the policy denies. An
example: a policy allows `read_file` only for a `path` under `/workspace/`. The decider sees
`{"path":"/workspace/a"}` and allows it. A client that holds the prefix `{"path":"/wor"}` holds a
call that the policy would block. The oracle must catch this, and the gateway must not produce it.

## 2. Measured current state (2026-11-14, `origin/main` 2d58afd6)

The oracle was instrumented temporarily and `tests/properties.rs` and `tests/fixtures.rs` were run
once (10 000 cases per format for P1).

- M1. The strict-prefix branch (a partial result that is a prefix but not equal) fired **9 times**.
  All 9 were the LangChain model, on OpenAI streams, through the parsed (`json_prefix`) branch.
  Examples: `{"v":"pihn"}` of `{"v":"pihnarwopuv"}`, `{}` of `{"v":"vgfpua"}`, `{"v":"CA"}` of
  `{"v":"CANARY-u"}`.
- M2. The raw `starts_with` branch (openai-python, openai-node) fired **0 times**. The
  anthropic-python model fired **0 times** (an interleaved Anthropic block is already the deviation
  `block_interleave`).
- M3. Every one of the 9 streams has the same shape. The interceptor forwards the upstream records
  verbatim after the decision. A function call's argument fragments are interleaved with a later
  tool-call entry that has no `function` body (a `custom` call). LangChain's
  `_convert_delta_to_message_chunk` reads `rtc["function"].get(...)` and raises `AttributeError`
  at that record (the model in `run_langchain`). The upstream bytes raise the same way, so the
  raise is excused. LangChain's snapshot at the raise holds only the fragments of the earlier
  records, so it holds a strict prefix of the decided call. `core_failed` was `false` in all 9.

So the gap is real today, not only in the oracle. With an argument-reading decider, the gateway
lets a LangChain client hold a call that the policy did not decide.

## 3. Decisions

| Id | Decision |
|----|----------|
| D1 | Scope: the oracle **and** the interceptor (Sven chose option 1 on 2026-11-14). An oracle-only change cannot pass honestly (M3). |
| D2 | Oracle rule: a strict-prefix partial result is accepted only when the decider gives the partial arguments the same verdict as the decided call. The decided call is `Allow` (only allowed calls are candidates), so the partial arguments must also be `Allow`. Rejecting every strict partial (the second option of the issue) was considered and rejected: it is stricter than I1 needs, and it needs the same interceptor fix. |
| D3 | Interceptor rule: a new canonical-form deviation in the OpenAI stream assembly (§ 5). It is a stream-level `on_failure`, as every § 4.3 deviation of SMA-749 is. |
| D4 | No change for Anthropic (M2, `block_interleave`) and none for non-stream bodies (a body has no fragments). |
| D5 | The test deciders gain one argument-reading decider (§ 6.1), which runs everywhere the existing three run. |

## 4. The oracle change

`check_i1` gets the decider that produced `decided`:

```rust
pub fn check_i1(format: Format, input: &[u8], out: &[u8], decided: &[(ToolCall, Decision)],
                core_failed: bool, decide: &dyn Fn(&ToolCall) -> Decision) -> Result<(), String>
```

The candidates keep the decided `ToolCall` next to its `ModelCall`, so the oracle can re-decide.

`arguments_match` with `partial`:

1. An exact match (the non-partial rules, including `""` against `{}`) is accepted, as today.
2. Otherwise, a prefix by the existing rule (`json_prefix` for a parsed value, `starts_with` for a
   raw string) is a **candidate** only.
3. The oracle builds a copy of the decided `ToolCall` with `arguments` replaced by the partial
   arguments in the form the core would give the decider:
   - a parsed model value: its compact JSON (`Value::to_string`), which is the form
     `ModelCall.arguments` already holds;
   - a raw string: the string itself, except that `""` becomes `{}` for kinds Function and
     LegacyFunctionCall (the core's rule, `complete_arguments`).
4. The candidate is accepted only when `decide(&partial_call) == Decision::Allow`.

Kind `other` keeps its current rule (arguments are not compared, the decided form is the raw entry).

All call sites pass the decider they used: `check_p1` and `check_all_deciders` in
`tests/properties.rs`, `every_fixture_holds_i1_for_every_client` in `tests/fixtures.rs`, and any
other caller. The doc comments of `check_i1`, `arguments_match` and the module header must say that
a partial result must keep the verdict, and why (SMA-752).

## 5. The interceptor change

The deviation closes M3. It is defined by what the client sees, not by the name of one SDK.

**Rule (OpenAI stream, per choice).** Call a tool-call entry **bodyless** when it has no
`function` object (`Fragment.function` is `None`): a `custom` entry, an entry with only `index`,

  ## Verdict: NEEDS REWORK
  The § 5 rule is correct for its own trigger, but it closes only one of at least five raise paths in the models. Each path is a record that the interceptor accepts and queues between two fragments of an allowed call. D2 accepts a strict prefix whenever the test decider allows it. So a green suite does not show I1 for SMA-752 policies. The proof that § 5 bites is a random red or a check of a metric only.
  
  Short file names below are listed with absolute paths under "Files cited" at the end.
  
  ## Findings
  
  ### BLOCKER
  
  - **§ 5 closes one of at least five mid-call raise paths** - The interceptor queues every frame behind an open hold (`interceptor.rs:309-317`). After the decision it forwards each frame verbatim. Each record below passes `classify.rs` and makes a model raise between two fragments of an allowed call:
    (a) A record with no `choices` key. `classify.rs:71` reads it as "no choices". openai-python raises `AttributeError` when `object` is `chat.completion.chunk` (`oracle.rs:571-573`). openai-node raises `TypeError` on any such record (`oracle.rs:680-682`).
    (b) A choice entry with no `delta` key (`classify.rs:95`). LangChain raises `KeyError` (`oracle.rs:867`). openai-python raises `AttributeError` (`oracle.rs:593`).
    (c) A later fragment with `"type": null` after `"type":"function"`. `opt_str` treats null as absent (`json.rs:215-220`), so `Check::apply` sees no type and no `repeated_type` (`assembly.rs:99`). openai-python's `accumulate_delta` replaces `type` with null (`oracle.rs:440-442`). It then raises `AssertionError` (`oracle.rs:595-598`). This is the reachable openai-python AssertionError path. The IndexError paths are unreachable because of `index_gap`.
    (d) A legacy `function_call` with an extra key whose JSON type changes between fragments, for example `"x":1` and then `"x":"s"`, or `true` and then `false`. `name_args` reads only `name` and `arguments` (`classify.rs:150-155`). LangChain copies the extra keys (`oracle.rs:879-881`), and `lc_merge_dicts` raises `TypeError` (`oracle.rs:808-810`, `826`). This partial is raw (`parsed: false`).
    In every case the upstream bytes raise the same way, so the raise is excused (`oracle.rs:164`), and `core_failed` is false. The current oracle accepts the strict prefix. M2's "0 times" comes from `streams.rs`, which never renders these shapes. It is not a property of the interceptor. § 7's non-goal ("LangChain is the only model that holds a strict prefix") rests on M2. Dropped records are not a path: under `block`, a record is dropped only when no hold is open, after `[DONE]`, or as `late_fragment` after the decision. openai-node finalize errors are not a path either: they come after every record is read, so the calls are complete. | Why it matters: After SMA-752, openai-python, openai-node and LangChain clients can still hold a call that the policy did not decide. § 1 says that the gateway must not produce this. | Suggested fix: Define § 5 by a property, not by one SDK. Between a call's first fragment and its choice's `finish_reason`, no forwarded record may make a model raise. While choice 0 assembles, make each of (a)-(d) a deviation, and keep the bodyless rule. For (c), count a present `type` key, null included, as the type fragment. For (d), allow only `name` and `arguments` in `function_call`. Add one `Quirk` per path to `streams.rs` so that P1 renders each shape.
  
  - **D2 makes the oracle's verdict depend on the test decider** - Under D2, `allow-all` and `block-by-name` accept every strict prefix. `block_by_argument` accepts every prefix that keeps `v` at 4 or more characters. M1's `{"v":"pihn"}` of `{"v":"pihnarwopuv"}` passes, but a policy `v == "pihnarwopuv"` denies it. Raw Function or Legacy partials such as `{"v":"ab` are not one JSON value. The core never gives such a string to a decider (`complete_arguments`, `assembly.rs:207-220`). So their verdict shows only how a test decider treats invalid JSON. The parent I1 (SMA-749 spec, lines 46-49) requires "the same ... arguments that the decider saw". That contradicts D2's reason "stricter than I1 needs". D2's other reason, "it needs the same interceptor fix", is true, and that fix is sufficient: all 9 M1 hits are M3, and § 5 removes M3. | Why it matters: A green suite then shows I1 only for the four test deciders. The gateway never asks the production decider about a partial, so it cannot keep the verdict for an arbitrary policy. | Suggested fix: Use option 2. Reject every strict partial for each kind whose arguments are compared, and keep the exact `""`/`{}` rule. A decider-free equivalent: assert that no excused raise point lies inside an allowed call's fragment span. With option 2, all 9 M1 hits red under every decider, so red 2 of § 6.4 becomes almost certain. Keep `block_by_argument` if you want more rewrite coverage, but the proof does not need it.
  
  ### MAJOR
  
  - **The proof that § 5 bites is random, and the new fixture cannot red I1** - Reds 2 and 4 depend on `openai_p1_and_p2_hold`. No `proptest-regressions` directory exists, so each run uses a new random seed. M1 saw 9 strict-prefix hits in one run, across all deciders. Under threshold 4 only some of them red. Of the three examples, `{}` reds, `{"v":"pihn"}` does not, and `{"v":"CA"}` is part of a `blocked_*` call that `block_by_argument` blocks by name. The § 5 fixture puts a blocked canary in the late fragment. Under three deciders, that call is blocked by name and the rewrite removes it, with or without § 5. Under `allow-all`, D2 accepts any prefix. So `every_fixture_holds_i1_for_every_client` stays green under mutation 4. Example: `read_file` with `{"v":"abcdefgh"}`, split as `{"v":"ab` and `cdefgh"}` around a `custom` entry. Put the canary in a separate call. Name this fixture's I1 failure as the deterministic red for mutation 4.
  
  - **The § 6.2 test can pass for the wrong reason, and red 1 cannot be measured as written** - `check_i1` runs all three OpenAI runners (`oracle.rs:160`). If call 1 (custom) is not `Allow`, or the decider blocks call 1's input, openai-python and openai-node hold call 1. `check_i1` then returns "runs an undecided or blocked call" on the current oracle, so red 1 does not red. Red 1 also does not compile: the test calls the new signature, and `warnings = "deny"` (`rs/Cargo.toml:291-292`) applies to test targets, so an unused `decide` parameter is an error. `ToolCall` is `#[non_exhaustive]` with no constructor (`types.rs:47-59`), so an integration test cannot build `decided` with a struct literal. After § 5, the interleaved stream deviates and gives no `Decide` action, so the interceptor cannot supply the calls either. | Why it matters: The only test that shows the verdict half bites can be green on the old oracle, or cannot be built. | Suggested fix: Make call 1 `Allow` with input that the decider allows. Assert that the error names `langchain` and call 0. Define red 1 as "decider passed as `_decide` and not used". That is the same state as red 3, so say this or drop one of the two. Build `ToolCall`s from `parse_body` (`lib.rs:20`, `BodyCalls.calls` is `pub`), then assign fields on a clone.

The interceptor checks only that `partial_json` is a string (`anthropic/stream.rs:292`), and it checks completeness only at the stop (line 323). A delta that ends inside a number makes the model raise in the block. It then holds `{}` of `{"n":10.5}`. The raise is excused. The generators never put a decimal number in an Anthropic input. `capitalise_args` adds only the integer `"Id":1` (`streams.rs:174`). | Why it matters: There are two possible outcomes. D4's reason (`block_interleave`) covers neither outcome. | Suggested fix: Measure jiter 2.3.0 in partial mode on `{"n":10.`. Then fix the model, or add a rule and a generator for it.

With § 5 under `on_failure = allow`, the deviating record goes into `proto.step` and is never emitted (`interceptor.rs:253-256`). Later records are forwarded unclassified. openai-python and openai-node then run call 0 without that fragment. For example, `{"a":1,` + (dropped `"b":2,`) + `"c":3}` becomes `{"a":1,"c":3}`. `observe_mode_is_bounded_and_parseable` checks only raises, so it does not show this. § 5 says only that the stream "switches to pass-through". | Why it matters: Two clients that worked before now get unenforced calls with changed arguments, and nothing reports it. | Suggested fix: State this trade-off in § 5, or forward the deviating record for this deviation when the stream switches to pass-through.
  
  - **Two I1 holes outside this spec have the same root cause** - (1) LangChain reads `chunk.choices` when `choices` is empty (`oracle.rs:859-862`). `classify.rs` ignores a top-level `chunk` key, and `chunk` is not in `CLASSIFIER_KEYS` (`json.rs:27-57`). It is forwarded, and the LangChain model runs a call that no decider saw, under every decider. (2) LangChain skips each record whose top-level `type` is `content.delta` (`oracle.rs:856-858`), but the interceptor applies its fragments. LangChain then runs arguments with a gap. This hole is directly relevant to argument policies. No generator renders either shape. | Why it matters: Hole 1 is worse than this spec's subject, because it lets a full undecided call through without SMA-752. Hole 2 is an argument mismatch that the prefix rule does not cover. | Suggested fix: Give both holes a home before SMA-752, in this spec or in the follow-up sweep. Add a generator quirk for each.
  
  ### MINOR
  
  - **"The call count at the first bodyless record" is ambiguous** - It can mean the count before the record, after it, or partway through its entries. Only "before" matches the rule text. "After" fails every multi-fragment custom call. "Partway" fails a function call that starts in the same record. | Suggested fix: Write "the number of calls that existed before this record was applied". For the body path, add a test that pins a no-op: `asm.apply` runs once per body (`openai/body.rs:75-76`).
  - **The rule is slightly too broad** - An empty later fragment (`"arguments":""`, `null`, or `"function":{}`) after the bodyless record is a deviation, but LangChain holds the full call. Otherwise the rule is correct for its trigger: same-record entries, `{"index":0}`-only entries and `"function": null` are all covered. | Suggested fix: Accept this and say so, or exempt fragments that add nothing.
  - **Partial form and candidate choice (only if D2 stays)** - A parsed partial is given to the decider as compact JSON, but the full call was decided on the raw upstream string. A string-matching decider then mixes "form changed" with "prefix changed". Matching is greedy first-fit and does not prefer an exact match (`oracle.rs:169-171`). This can give a false Err when two allowed calls share choice, kind and name. The re-decided copy also takes `id` and `position` from whichever candidate matched. | Suggested fix: Require the test deciders to be pure and to parse JSON. Match exact candidates before prefix candidates.
  - **`json_prefix` accepts shapes that are not prefixes** - It accepts any subset of object keys in any order, and arrays where every element is cut (`oracle.rs:115-116`). A text prefix can cut only the last value. Under D2, these shapes pass when the verdict stays. Under option 2, this does not matter.

So no decider ever tests an allowed Other call against arguments. | Suggested fix: State this as a non-goal, and add the limit for SMA-752 policies that read Other arguments.
  - **The doc target does not exist** - "The SMA-749 § 4.3 list in this crate's docs" does not exist: the crate `README.md` has no § 4.3 list. | Suggested fix: Name the file.
  - **The `arguments_match` unit test runs many times** - `support/` is compiled into every integration-test binary (`support/mod.rs`), so a `#[test]` there runs once per binary. | Suggested fix: Put the test in one test file.
